title: One-way state generators versus EFI pairs
formal: Does the existence of EFI pairs imply the existence of efficiently verifiable one-way state generators in the ordinary quantum circuit model defined below? Both primitives have uniform polynomial-time honest algorithms and security against polynomial-size quantum circuits with classical nonuniformity. The implication is between existence assertions; no oracle is supplied to any algorithm.
why: The question asks whether computational indistinguishability alone supplies quantum search hardness with an efficiently checkable secret. Its answer determines whether two central minimal assumptions for quantum cryptography have the same power once the cost of verification is included.
status_note: Source-open in the 2024 comparison, with the explicitly selected ordinary-model EFI branch and classical-advice convention. Subsequent equivalence permits unbounded verification, and the checked negative result is oracle-relative. An August 2026 learning paper also concerns inefficient verification and different security conventions. Bounded checks on 2026-09-16 found no matching ordinary-model resolution; no exhaustive current-openness claim is made.

importance.reason: A basic comparison of minimal quantum cryptographic assumptions, connecting indistinguishability, search hardness and efficient verification; the distinction affects which primitives can be based on the weakest known quantum resources.

sentences: EFI pairs are easy to generate quantum states that are statistically different but computationally difficult to distinguish.
One-way state generators instead hide a classical key while allowing an efficient quantum verifier to check candidate keys.
This card asks whether existence of EFI pairs already guarantees such an efficiently verifiable generator in the ordinary model.
The adversary may have polynomial classical advice and polynomially many independently generated copies of the hidden-key state.
Known equivalence with unlimited verification and separation relative to a quantum oracle leave distinct issues from this precisely selected implication.

definitions:
The security parameter is an integer \(\lambda\ge1\), supplied as the unary string \(1^\lambda\). A negligible function is a map \(\nu:\mathbb N_{>0}\to[0,1]\) such that, for every integer \(c\ge1\), eventually \(\nu(\lambda)\le\lambda^{-c}\). Each security quantifier may have its own negligible function. Polynomial bounds have fixed constants and exponents independent of \(\lambda\).

An \(m\)-qubit state is a positive semidefinite complex matrix of trace one on \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}\). Algorithms use quantum circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), preparation of zero qubits, computational-basis measurement, classical control and discarding qubits. Here \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\). Classical inputs and outputs are bit strings. All gate applications, classical computation and input/output operations are charged. A uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm has one deterministic classical polynomial-time circuit generator, and its circuit size and classical control time are polynomial in the input length on every branch. Honest algorithms receive no advice. Their security-parameter-dependent lengths are positive, polynomially bounded and polynomial-time computable.

An adversary is any family of polynomial-size circuits in this model, with arbitrary polynomial-size classical descriptions depending on \(\lambda\). Equivalently it may use polynomially many classical advice bits depending only on \(\lambda\), independently of the sampled secret or challenge bit. It may prepare quantum work registers from zero but receives no arbitrary quantum advice. There is no oracle or uncharged computation. The descriptions of all honest algorithms are public.

An EFI pair consists of one uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithm \(G\) with output \(m(\lambda)\) qubits. Write \(\rho_{b,\lambda}\) for the mixed output of \(G(1^\lambda,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). The following two requirements hold:
\[
\exists p\ \exists\lambda_0\ \forall\lambda\ge\lambda_0:
\quad \frac12\|\rho_{0,\lambda}-\rho_{1,\lambda}\|_1\ge\frac1{p(\lambda)},
\]
where \(p\) is a positive polynomial, and, for every adversary \(D\), its distinguishing advantage
\[
\left|\Pr[D(1^\lambda,\rho_{0,\lambda})=1]
-\Pr[D(1^\lambda,\rho_{1,\lambda})=1]\right|
\]
is negligible. The trace norm is \(\|X\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{X^\dagger X}\). The distinguishing experiment supplies one challenge state. Its preparation randomness and all measurements are included in the probabilities.

An efficiently verifiable one-way state generator consists of three uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms \(\mathrm{KeyGen},\mathrm{StateGen},\mathrm{Ver}\). The first, on \(1^\lambda\), samples a classical key \(k\in\{0,1\}^{\kappa(\lambda)}\). The second, on \((1^\lambda,k)\), outputs an \(m(\lambda)\)-qubit state \(\sigma_{k,\lambda}\), which may be mixed. The third, on \((1^\lambda,k',\sigma)\), outputs an acceptance bit; a key of the wrong length is rejected. Correctness requires
\[
\Pr_{k\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda)}
 [\mathrm{Ver}(1^\lambda,k,\sigma_{k,\lambda})=1]\ge1-\nu(\lambda)
\]
for some negligible \(\nu\). This is averaged over the generated key, not a promise of correctness for every bit string.

Security requires that, for every positive integer-valued polynomial copy bound \(t(\lambda)\) and every adversary \(A\), the following success probability is negligible:
\[
\Pr\!\left[
\mathrm{Ver}(1^\lambda,k',\sigma_{k,\lambda})=1:
\ k\leftarrow\mathrm{KeyGen}(1^\lambda),\
 k'\leftarrow A(1^\lambda,\sigma_{k,\lambda}^{\otimes t(\lambda)})
\right].
\]
Conditioned on \(k\), all copies are produced by independent runs of \(\mathrm{StateGen}\). The verifier's copy is fresh and independent of the copies supplied to \(A\). The probability includes key generation, state preparation and all measurements. The adversary wins by producing any accepted key, not necessarily the original key. In particular the verifier must be efficient; allowing it unlimited time defines a different primitive.

The proposition quantifies over existence of complete schemes, with their own polynomial lengths and running-time bounds. It does not prescribe a fixed transformation or loss of security from a given EFI generator. A counterexample relative to an added oracle, or impossibility for one restricted form of transformation, does not by itself negate this ordinary-model existence implication.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of this existence implication, or a complete Lean proof of its negation in the stated ordinary model. All correctness, polynomial-time and asymptotic security requirements must match the definitions, including efficient verification and classical rather than quantum advice. An equivalence with generators whose verifier has unlimited running time, an oracle-relative separation or a restriction on black-box constructions alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Question 4 compares one-way state generators with EFI pairs and, separately, pseudorandom state generators. This card selects the EFI comparison. It fixes mixed outputs, average correctness over generated keys and the usual polynomial-copy security experiment, and isolates the EFI-to-efficiently-verifiable direction. The separate pseudorandom-state comparison is not silently identified with this target.

The source uses nonuniform adversaries without fully spelling out an advice convention. This card chooses polynomial classical advice and uniform honest algorithms, matching the explicit adversary convention used by Batra and Jain. It does not assert equivalence to definitions with arbitrary quantum advice.

Batra and Jain prove that EFI pairs and statistically verifiable one-way state generators are equivalent, where the verifier need not run efficiently. In this convention an efficiently verifiable generator is a special case and therefore implies EFI pairs. Their converse produces the more general primitive and does not provide the efficient verifier required here.

Behera and coauthors exhibit a unitary-oracle world with EFI pairs but no efficiently verifiable one-way state generators. This separates the oracle-relative notions and rules out implications that work in every such world. It is not a proof that the ordinary-model existence implication written on this card is false.

The August 2026 learning paper relates mixed-state learning hardness to inefficiently verifiable generators. Its stated definitions use uniform adversaries and correctness for every key, which differ from the conventions here. Neither that equivalence nor its oracle separation is being imported as a resolution of this target.

checked_sources: Read TQC 2024 Question 4, Section 2.1, Definitions 1 and 9 and footnote 8. Mixed outputs and average correctness are essential; copied states in verification and the adversary experiment are prepared independently.

Read Batra–Jain arXiv:2404.03220v4 Introduction and Definitions 14–17. They explicitly use polynomial classical advice. Corollary 2 and Theorem 4 concern statistically verifiable generators with unbounded verification, and imply the known efficiently-verifiable-OWSG to EFI direction in the selected convention. This review checked statements and model, not the full equivalence proof.

Read Behera et al. arXiv:2410.03453v3 Section 1.1 and Definition 2.2. Corollary 1.2 is explicitly relative to a unitary oracle. The card selects the ordinary model and does not present an oracle separation as its negation; no full oracle-separation proof audit was performed.

Read Cojocaru–Lewis arXiv:2608.14331v1 Introduction and Section 2.3. Inefficient verification is explicit; uniform adversaries and correctness for every key differ from this card. Its cited exponential-loss consequence is not used as the best general EFI equivalence, since the Batra–Jain classical-advice convention already gives a stronger equivalence.

Bounded subsequent primary-source searches through 2026-09-16 located these inefficient-verifier and oracle results, not an ordinary-model implication with the efficient verifier stipulated here. The EFI and classical-advice selections are documented rather than claimed equivalent to the entire parenthetical source question.
